extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy, public policy makers, and historians of colonial trade
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Adam Smith's evaluative principles about colonies, slavery, and the effects of exclusive (monopoly) trade on national industry, capital allocation, and public welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition of slaves under arbitrary vs free government
rubrics_metrics.description: That the condition of a slave is better under an arbitrary than under a free government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: In an arbitrary government magistrates more readily intermeddle to protect slaves from masters' violence; such protection makes masters treat slaves with more gentleness and respect, producing more faithful and useful servants. Example/anecdote: Roman emperor Augustus ordering Vidius Pollio to emancipate a slave and punish the master for cruelty; under the republic such protection would not have been possible. Explanation includes political mechanics: in a free country masters (who may be assembly members or electors) make magistrates cautious about interfering with private property, reducing slave protection; in arbitrary regimes intermeddling is usual and easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentle management increases a slave's usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentle usage renders the slave not only more faithful, but more intelligent, and, therefore, upon a double account, more useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: Treatment affects productivity — gentler care approaches the slave toward the condition of a free servant, producing integrity and attachment to the master's interest. Implication: systems of governance and law that restrain extreme cruelty can raise the productive value of forced labor by improving behaviour and intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of colonial stock/capital matters for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The stock which has improved the sugar colonies of France has been raised almost entirely from the gradual improvement and cultivation of those colonies; English colonial improvement has in a great measure depended on capital sent out from England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation: Local accumulation and reinvestment (produce of the soil and industry of colonists) indicates superior local conduct and sustainable improvement, whereas reliance on capital exported from the mother country indicates prosperity owing to external riches. Implication: colonies that internally generate and reinvest surplus are likely to show better long-term management and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonies often founded by domestic injustice or folly rather than policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Folly and injustice seem to have been the principles which presided over and directed the first project of establishing those colonies; the folly of hunting after gold and silver mines, and the injustice of coveting the possession of a country whose harmless natives had received the adventurers with kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: Many colonial settlements were the result of persecution, exile, adventurism, or private daring rather than deliberate, wise policy from metropolitan governments (examples: puritans to New England, catholics to Maryland, quakers to Pennsylvania, Portuguese Jews to Brazil). Implication for evaluation: the origin motive of a colony influences its character and governance; praise for policy should be tempered by recognizing these non-strategic origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive trade (monopoly) diminishes enjoyments and industry
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive trade of the mother countries tends to diminish, or at least to keep down below what they would otherwise rise to, both the enjoyments and industry of all those nations in general, and of the American colonies in particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: Monopoly makes colony produce dearer abroad (less consumption) and foreign produce dearer in the colonies (less consumption there), thereby cramping industry and enjoyment. It confines colonies to a single market rather than leaving many open markets, which is worse than mere exclusion from one market. The surplus produce of the colonies is the source of increased enjoyments and industry for Europe; exclusive trade reduces that surplus's abundance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly confers a relative, not necessarily absolute, advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: This advantage, however, will, perhaps, be found to be rather what may be called a relative than an absolute advantage, and to give a superiority to the country which enjoys it, rather by depressing the industry and produce of other countries, than by raising those of that particular country above what they would naturally rise to in the case of a free trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tobacco from Maryland comes cheaper to England by virtue of the monopoly, but under free trade tobacco might be cheaper everywhere and England would not have a superior absolute advantage — only a relative one. Implication: policy-makers should distinguish temporary or comparative gains from true absolute improvement in national welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly attracts capital and shifts its allocation across trades
rubrics_metrics.description: When, by the act of navigation, England assumed to herself the monopoly of the colony trade, foreign capitals were necessarily withdrawn from it and English capital had to carry on the whole; this drew capital from other branches of trade to the colony trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects: The high profitability of monopolized colonial trade draws capital away from other trades, reducing competition there and altering the direction of national manufactures toward the monopoly market. Over time, this revulsion of capital causes decay in other foreign-trade branches and reshapes the structure of industrial production (manufactures become tailored to the monopolized colonial market rather than nearer European markets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly raises the ordinary rate of profit above its natural level
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopoly of the colony trade...necessarily raised the rate of profit in that branch; by lessening competition it raised the rate of British profit higher than it otherwise would have been, both in that and in all the other branches of British trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: Higher ordinary profits make domestic goods dearer (because merchants need to obtain higher profit), subjecting the country to absolute disadvantages (buying and selling dearer, producing less) and relative disadvantages (other countries can undersell in foreign markets). Policymakers should account for the distortion of profit rates when evaluating monopolistic trade policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonies typically supply little military force and can be net fiscal drains
rubrics_metrics.description: The European colonies of America have never yet furnished any military force for the defence of the mother country... The taxes which have been levied upon those of other European nations, upon those of England in particular, have seldom been equal to the expense laid out upon them in time of peace, and never sufficient to defray that which they occasioned in time of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment: Unlike some ancient colonies, modern European colonies in America rarely provide military support and often cost more to maintain than the revenue they produce, with exceptions such as Spanish and Portuguese colonies. This should be factored into cost–benefit analyses of colonial empires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most advantageous employment of capital measured by productive labour maintained (frequency of returns)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most advantageous employment of any capital to the country to which it belongs, is that which maintains there the greatest quantity of productive labour, and increases the most the annual produce of the land and labour of that country... the quantity of productive labour which any capital employed in the foreign trade of consumption can maintain, is exactly in proportion to the frequency of its returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical metric: Evaluate capital uses by how much productive labour they keep in constant employment; for foreign trade of consumption, more frequent returns (e.g., two or three returns per year versus one) effectively multiply the labour supported by the same capital. Policy implication: when comparing trades or investments, prioritize those that maximize maintained productive labour, not merely nominal profit.
